questions.stem: As tribune in 133 BCE, Tiberius Gracchus proposed a law to:
options: enforce the limit on holdings of public land and give the surplus to poor citizens
give full Roman citizenship to all the Latin and Italian allies who served in the army
transfer the jury courts from the senators to the equestrian order
sell grain to every citizen in Rome each month at a low fixed price
questions.explanation: Tiberius revived the old legal limit on occupying ager publicus and set up a land commission of three to distribute reclaimed land in small allotments. Citizenship for allies, jury reform and the grain law were associated with his brother Gaius.

questions.stem: Plutarch reports that Tiberius Gracchus was moved to act after seeing the countryside of Etruria worked by foreign slaves. The concern behind his land law was that:
options: the senate wanted to sell off public land to raise money for new wars abroad
fewer small farmers meant fewer men qualified to serve in the legions
slaves were about to revolt and seize control of the city of Rome
the Etruscans had stopped paying their taxes to the Roman treasury
questions.explanation: Soldiers had to own property, so the decline of small farms, as wealthy landowners built slave-worked estates, shrank Rome's pool of recruits. Settling poor citizens on public land was meant to restore that base.

questions.stem: When the tribune Marcus Octavius vetoed his land bill, Tiberius Gracchus responded by:
options: appealing to the consuls to arrest Octavius for blocking the people's will
having the assembly vote Octavius out of office, which was unprecedented
asking the senate to declare Octavius an enemy of the Roman state
withdrawing the bill and proposing a smaller one approved by the senate
questions.explanation: Removing a fellow tribune by popular vote had no precedent and seemed to attack the sacrosanct office itself. Tiberius argued that a tribune who acted against the people forfeited his position.

questions.stem: Tiberius Gracchus sought re-election as tribune for 132 BCE and was killed, with many supporters, by senators led by Scipio Nasica. The main significance of his death was that:
options: violence was now used to settle a political dispute inside the city
the land commission was abolished and its lands returned to the rich
the tribunate was abolished and replaced by a board of senators
Rome's allies rose in revolt to avenge Tiberius's death at once
questions.explanation: Plutarch calls this the first civil strife in Rome since the kings to end in bloodshed, and it set a precedent for political killing. The land commission in fact continued its work after his death, and the tribunate survived.

questions.stem: As tribune in 123 and 122 BCE, Gaius Gracchus passed laws that:
options: freed all slaves in Italy who had worked on public land for ten years
provided subsidised grain and gave the extortion court juries to the equites
made him dictator for life and gave him command of every Roman army
abolished the senate's control over the provinces and gave it to the two consuls
questions.explanation: Gaius's grain law sold grain to citizens at a low fixed price, and his jury law placed equites rather than senators on the court that tried governors for extortion. He also proposed colonies and citizenship for the Latins.

questions.stem: Gaius Gracchus gave the juries of the extortion court to the equites. Historians see this as a significant change because it:
options: made governors answerable to the Roman allies instead of the courts
set senators and equites against each other over control of the provinces
allowed equites to be elected consul without serving in any other office
ended the senate's right to try any case involving a Roman citizen
questions.explanation: Equites, many of them tax-collecting businessmen, could now judge senatorial governors, which created a lasting conflict within the elite over the courts and provincial profits. Sulla later returned the courts to senators.

questions.stem: Gaius Marius was described as a novus homo (‘new man’) because he:
options: had been born a slave and later gained his freedom
came from a patrician family that had lost its wealth
had no senatorial ancestors yet rose to the consulship
was the first general to command a Roman fleet
questions.explanation: A novus homo was the first of his family to enter the Senate, and the term is used especially of such men who reached the consulship. Marius came from an equestrian family of Arpinum, so his election as consul in 107 BCE broke into the nobility's hold on the office. Sulla, by contrast, was from an impoverished patrician family.

questions.stem: In 107 BCE, Marius gained the command against Jugurtha in Numidia when:
options: the senate dismissed Metellus for taking bribes from King Jugurtha
Sulla resigned the command and recommended Marius to replace him
the consuls drew lots and Marius was given the province of Numidia by chance
the people's assembly voted it to him, overriding the senate's choice
questions.explanation: The senate had extended Metellus's command, but a tribune's law in the assembly transferred it to Marius. Using the assembly to override the senate on a military command became a recurring tactic.

questions.stem: For the war against Jugurtha, Marius enlisted volunteers from:
options: the equites, who served as cavalry at their own expense
the capite censi, citizens with too little property to qualify for service
the Italian allies, who were all promised full Roman citizenship after the war
the slaves of Rome, who were promised freedom after the war
questions.explanation: Sallust says Marius enrolled the capite censi, the ‘head count’ who owned little or no property, rather than relying on the traditional property-based levy. These men looked to their general for pay and land.

questions.stem: Why did the recruitment of propertyless volunteers contribute to the fall of the Republic?
options: it allowed the senate to control every soldier directly through the public treasury
it ended the use of Italian allies in the Roman legions altogether
soldiers looked to their generals rather than the state for land on discharge
it made the army too small to defend Italy against foreign invaders
questions.explanation: Because the state made no regular provision for veterans, soldiers depended on their commanders to win them land, which bound armies to individual generals. Sulla, Pompey and Caesar later relied on that loyalty.

questions.stem: Marius was elected consul every year from 104 to 100 BCE because:
options: Sulla, his rival, had been exiled and no other candidate stood against him
Rome feared invasion by the Cimbri and Teutones and wanted him in command
the senate had suspended elections after the death of Gaius Gracchus
he had marched on Rome and forced the assembly to elect him each year
questions.explanation: After heavy defeats by the Germanic Cimbri and Teutones, voters kept re-electing Marius, who destroyed them at Aquae Sextiae in 102 and Vercellae in 101. Repeated consulships broke the custom of intervals between terms.

questions.stem: Military reforms traditionally attributed to Marius include:
options: replacing the legion with a Greek-style phalanx armed with long Macedonian spears
paying soldiers in land grants in Italy as soon as they enlisted
abolishing the cavalry and relying only on allied archers
giving each legion an eagle standard and making soldiers carry their own kit
questions.explanation: Marius is credited with making the eagle the standard of every legion, which strengthened its identity, and with making soldiers carry their own equipment, earning them the nickname ‘Marius's mules’. Land on discharge, not on enlistment, was what veterans hoped for.

questions.stem: As Marius's quaestor in Numidia, Sulla arranged the capture of Jugurtha in 105 BCE. According to Plutarch, this caused rivalry between them because:
options: Marius had Sulla arrested for negotiating with King Bocchus without any orders
Sulla killed Jugurtha before Marius could lead him in a triumph
the senate gave Sulla a triumph and refused one to Marius
Sulla wore a signet ring showing the surrender, claiming credit for himself
questions.explanation: Plutarch says Sulla had a ring engraved with Bocchus handing over Jugurtha and used it as his seal, which annoyed Marius, who triumphed over Jugurtha. The rivalry grew into civil war.

questions.stem: In 88 BCE, after a tribune transferred his command against Mithridates to Marius, Sulla:
options: joined Marius as his deputy for the campaign in the East
marched on Rome with his army, the first Roman to do so
accepted the decision and retired to his estates in Campania
appealed to the senate, which restored his command by decree
questions.explanation: Sulla persuaded his soldiers, who feared losing the profits of an eastern war, to follow him against the city, and he drove out Marius and Sulpicius. Bringing an army into Rome set a dangerous precedent.

questions.stem: Appian says that when Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE, all his officers except one quaestor refused to follow him, but his soldiers obeyed. This suggests that:
options: the soldiers' loyalty was now to their general, not to the state
the senatorial officers supported Marius and joined his army
the soldiers had been promised Roman citizenship by Sulla
Sulla's march was approved in advance by the whole senate
questions.explanation: The officers, men of senatorial background, recoiled from attacking Rome, while the rank and file followed the general who promised them reward. The episode shows the change in the army's loyalties that made civil war possible.

questions.stem: After winning the civil war in 82 BCE, Sulla was appointed dictator. His dictatorship differed from the traditional office because it:
options: lasted only six months and was limited to fighting a single war
had no fixed time limit and was for writing laws and restoring the state
was shared with Pompey and Crassus as an equal board of three joint dictators
was granted by the Italian allies rather than by any Roman authority
questions.explanation: The traditional dictatorship lasted at most six months in an emergency and had not been used for over a century, but Sulla's had no set term and was meant to remake the constitution. He nevertheless laid it down and retired before his death in 78.

questions.stem: Sulla's proscriptions were:
options: edicts forbidding generals to bring their armies into Italy
lists of senators entitled to command armies in the provinces
lists of named enemies who could be killed, with their property seized
laws banning the sale of grain in Rome at prices below the normal market price
questions.explanation: Names posted in the Forum could be killed for a reward, their property was confiscated, and their sons and grandsons were barred from office. Many were wealthy victims, and Sulla's supporters, such as Crassus, profited.

questions.stem: Sulla's reforms to restore senatorial power included:
options: restricting the tribunes and returning the jury courts to senators
abolishing the consulship and giving its powers to the censors
restoring the equites' control of the extortion court juries for good
allowing tribunes to propose laws without the senate's approval
questions.explanation: Sulla barred ex-tribunes from higher office and limited their ability to legislate, returned the courts to an enlarged senate and regulated the cursus honorum. Pompey and Crassus restored the tribunes' powers in 70 BCE.

questions.stem: Sulla used force to restore the senate's authority, then resigned and retired. Many historians argue that his career weakened the Republic because:
options: he abolished the senate and the assemblies before he retired
he named Pompey as his heir and made him dictator for life
he gave the tribunes unlimited power to veto senatorial decrees
his example showed that an army could be used to seize power in Rome
questions.explanation: Sulla's reforms aimed to strengthen the senate, but his march on Rome, civil war and proscriptions showed others how power could be taken by force. His constitutional settlement was largely undone within a decade.

questions.stem: In 83 BCE the young Pompey, who held no office, joined Sulla's side by:
options: leading the Italian allies in a revolt against Marius and Cinna
raising a private army of three legions from his family's clients in Picenum
persuading the senate to give him command of the consular armies
being elected tribune of the plebs and passing a law to recall Sulla from the East
questions.explanation: Pompey, aged about 23 and not even a senator, raised legions from his father's veterans and clients, and Sulla later hailed him as ‘Magnus’. Commanding armies without office was the first of his breaches of constitutional norms.

questions.stem: Pompey's election as consul for 70 BCE broke the rules of the cursus honorum because he:
options: had held no previous magistracy and was below the legal age
was a patrician, and both consuls that year had to be plebeians
had already served as consul twice within the previous ten years
was still dictator and could not hold another office at once
questions.explanation: Pompey went straight to the consulship on the strength of his military record and his army, without serving as quaestor or praetor. As consul with Crassus he restored the powers of the tribunes that Sulla had removed.

questions.stem: The Lex Gabinia of 67 BCE gave Pompey:
options: an extraordinary command over the whole Mediterranean against the pirates
the governorship of Spain, which he ruled through legates from Rome
the dictatorship for a single year to restore order in Rome after Clodius's death
command of the war against Mithridates in place of Lucullus
questions.explanation: The law gave Pompey vast resources and authority across the Mediterranean coasts, and he cleared the pirates within a few months. The Mithridatic command came the next year under the Lex Manilia.

questions.stem: In 52 BCE, after Clodius was killed and the senate house burned, Pompey was made sole consul. Why was this a breach of constitutional norms?
options: the consulship was meant to be shared, and he also held Spain through legates
Pompey had never held the consulship before and was still below the legal age
the senate had no power to appoint any consul during a state of emergency
Pompey was a tribune at the time and could not hold two offices
questions.explanation: Collegiality was a basic principle of the Republic, and Pompey was at the same time governing Spain through deputies while staying near Rome. The senate's optimates accepted this to restore order and to draw Pompey away from Caesar.

questions.stem: The ‘First Triumvirate’ formed in about 60 BCE was:
options: a court of three senators that tried cases of treason
an informal political alliance of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar
a legal board of three created by a law of the assembly
a military command shared by three consuls against Parthia
questions.explanation: Unlike the Second Triumvirate, it had no legal basis: it was a private agreement to combine Pompey's prestige and veterans, Crassus's wealth and Caesar's political skill. Pompey's marriage to Caesar's daughter Julia sealed it.

questions.stem: As consul in 59 BCE, Caesar passed his laws through the assembly despite his colleague Bibulus, who:
options: resigned the consulship and fled to Pompey's camp in Spain
was exiled by Caesar for opposing the land law for Pompey's many veterans
withdrew to his house and declared he was watching the skies for omens
vetoed every law and was supported by an army raised by the senate
questions.explanation: After being driven from the Forum, Bibulus stayed at home and announced unfavourable omens, which in theory made Caesar's laws invalid. Suetonius reports the joke that the year was the consulship of Julius and Caesar.

questions.stem: The First Triumvirate collapsed in the years after 54 BCE mainly because:
options: Julia died and Crassus was killed at Carrhae, leaving Pompey and Caesar as rivals
Caesar was defeated by Vercingetorix and lost the support of his army
Pompey retired from politics and gave his legions to Caesar
the senate passed a new law making all private alliances between politicians illegal
questions.explanation: The death of Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, in 54 and of Crassus fighting the Parthians in 53 removed two bonds holding the alliance together. Pompey moved closer to the optimates, who feared Caesar.

questions.stem: In 63 BCE, Caesar was elected to the important priesthood of:
options: pontifex maximus
rex sacrorum
chief Vestal
augur of Jupiter
questions.explanation: Caesar won the election as pontifex maximus against more senior rivals, reportedly with heavy borrowing and bribery. The office gave him prestige and a residence on the Sacred Way.

questions.stem: Caesar's conquest of Gaul between 58 and 50 BCE strengthened his position in Rome mainly because it:
options: allowed him to return to Rome as a private citizen with full immunity
gave him great wealth, military glory and a battle-hardened, loyal army
made him consul for ten years without the need for another election
ended his dependence on Crassus, who had paid for the whole campaign
questions.explanation: The Gallic Wars, culminating in the defeat of Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BCE, made Caesar enormously rich and famous and gave him legions loyal to him personally. His enemies wanted to strip him of his command and prosecute him.

questions.stem: Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War describe his campaigns in the third person. A historian should treat them with caution because:
options: they were composed two centuries after the Gallic Wars
Caesar was not present at any of the battles he described
Caesar wrote them to justify his actions to readers in Rome
they were written by Gallic chiefs who hated the Romans
questions.explanation: The Commentaries are an eyewitness account by the commander himself, valuable for detail, but their plain style and third-person narration make his decisions seem reasonable and his wars justified. Their purpose was political as well as historical.

questions.stem: In January 49 BCE, Caesar began the civil war by:
options: sailing to Egypt to seize the grain supply
marching on Rome from his province of Spain
crossing the Rubicon into Italy with his army
attacking Pompey's camp at Pharsalus in Greece
questions.explanation: The Rubicon marked the boundary of Caesar's province; bringing an army across it into Italy was an act of war against the state. The senate had demanded he give up his command, and he feared prosecution if he returned as a private citizen.

questions.stem: Caesar's relationship with Cleopatra VII influenced events because:
options: he married her in Rome and adopted her son as his heir in his will
he backed her claim to Egypt's throne, and her presence in Rome fuelled suspicion
she lent him the Egyptian fleet that defeated Pompey's forces at the battle of Pharsalus
she persuaded him to make Alexandria the capital of the Roman empire
questions.explanation: Caesar fought the Alexandrian War to place Cleopatra on the throne, and her stay in Rome from 46 BCE, along with a gilded statue of her in the temple of Venus Genetrix, fed fears that he wanted to rule like a Hellenistic king. His will adopted Octavian, not Caesarion.

questions.stem: In early 44 BCE, Caesar was named dictator perpetuo (dictator in perpetuity). This alarmed many senators because:
options: it was granted by Cleopatra, who claimed authority over Rome
it ended any hope that his rule was temporary and pointed to monarchy
it gave Mark Antony command of every army in the Roman provinces
it abolished the senate and gave its powers to the tribal assembly
questions.explanation: A lifelong dictatorship looked like kingship in all but name, especially after Antony offered Caesar a diadem at the Lupercalia. Caesar refused it publicly, but suspicion of monarchy helped unite the conspirators.

questions.stem: Julius Caesar was assassinated on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BCE by conspirators led by:
options: Cicero and Cato
Brutus and Cassius
Antony and Lepidus
Pompey and Crassus
questions.explanation: Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus led the conspiracy, and Caesar was killed at a senate meeting in the Curia of Pompey. Antony and Lepidus were Caesar's supporters, Pompey and Crassus were already dead, and Cato had died in 46.

questions.stem: In 44 BCE, Gaius Octavius became Caesar's heir when:
options: Cleopatra recognised him as the guardian of Caesarion
Caesar's will adopted him as his son and main heir
the senate chose him to succeed Caesar as dictator
Antony named him his deputy in the consulship
questions.explanation: Caesar's great-nephew, aged 18, was adopted in the will and took the name Gaius Julius Caesar, giving him the name and the loyalty of Caesar's veterans. The senate gave him no such office.

questions.stem: Unlike the First Triumvirate, the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus:
options: gave each member the title of king in his own provinces
was established by law, the Lex Titia of 43 BCE, for five years
was a secret private agreement that the senate and people never discovered
was formed to defend the Republic against the Gauls
questions.explanation: The Lex Titia created the triumvirs ‘for restoring the state’ with powers above the magistrates, making it a legal dictatorship of three. The first alliance had been a private, informal arrangement.

questions.stem: In 36 BCE, Lepidus lost his place in the Second Triumvirate when:
options: Cleopatra persuaded Antony to replace him with her son Caesarion
he resigned to become consul after the defeat of Sextus Pompeius
his troops in Sicily deserted to Octavian, who stripped him of power
he was killed by Mark Antony's agents during the Parthian campaign
questions.explanation: After the defeat of Sextus Pompeius, Lepidus tried to claim Sicily, but his legions went over to Octavian, who removed him from power while letting him keep the office of pontifex maximus. The triumvirate became a contest between Octavian and Antony.

questions.stem: In 32 BCE, Octavian seized Mark Antony's will from the Vestal Virgins and read parts of it to the senate. According to Plutarch, the will said that Antony:
options: intended to restore the Republic once he returned
wished to be buried in Alexandria beside Cleopatra
planned to make Octavian his heir and successor
had been secretly plotting with the Parthian king
questions.explanation: The burial wish and legacies to Cleopatra's children were used to suggest that Antony had abandoned Rome for Egypt. Seizing a will from the Vestals was itself illegal, which shows how far Octavian would go for propaganda.

questions.stem: In 32 BCE, Rome declared war on Cleopatra, not on Mark Antony. Octavian chose this approach mainly because it:
options: allowed him to avoid fighting Antony, whom he planned to forgive
was required by a treaty that made Cleopatra a friend of Rome
let the senate stay neutral while Octavian fought Egypt alone
presented the conflict as a foreign war rather than another civil war
questions.explanation: Romans were weary of civil war, so casting Cleopatra as a foreign threat and Antony as her captive allowed Octavian to rally Italy behind him, including through the oath of loyalty of 32. Antony was still treated as an enemy in practice.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE:
options: Pompey was defeated by Caesar and fled to Egypt
Octavian's fleet, commanded by Agrippa, defeated Antony and Cleopatra
Antony defeated Octavian, who escaped back to Italy with only a few ships
Brutus and Cassius were defeated by Antony and Octavian
questions.explanation: Agrippa's fleet defeated Antony off western Greece, and Cleopatra's squadron broke away with Antony following. Philippi in 42 BCE was the defeat of Brutus and Cassius, and Pharsalus in 48 BCE was Pompey's.

questions.stem: In the settlement of January 27 BCE, Octavian:
options: abolished the consulship and took the title of king, with a diadem
retired from public life and left the government of Rome to Agrippa and the senate
made himself dictator for life, as Caesar had done in 44 BCE
returned the state to senate and people, but kept the provinces with most legions
questions.explanation: Octavian ‘restored’ the Republic in name while receiving, for ten years, the provinces where most of the legions were stationed, and he took the name Augustus. He avoided the dictatorship and kingship that had doomed Caesar.

questions.stem: In the Res Gestae, Augustus says that after 27 BCE he excelled all in auctoritas (influence) but had no more potestas (power) than his colleagues in each magistracy. A historian should note that this claim:
options: was a private letter that Augustus never intended to be made public
is Augustus's own account, which plays down the legions and powers he held
was written by his enemies to show that he had no real influence in Rome
proves that the Republic was fully restored with equal magistrates
questions.explanation: The Res Gestae was Augustus's self-presentation, set up at his mausoleum, so it stresses legality and moral authority while passing over his control of the armies and his extraordinary powers. It is valuable evidence for how he wished to be seen.

questions.stem: In the settlement of 23 BCE, Augustus gave up the consulship he had held every year since 31 BCE and received:
options: tribunician power for life and imperium greater than other governors'
the dictatorship for ten years and command of the Praetorian Guard
the title of king of Italy and the right to name his successor
the office of censor for life and control of the treasury of Saturn
questions.explanation: Tribunician power gave him the tribunes' rights without holding the office, and his greater imperium gave him authority over the provinces. Resigning the consulship also opened that office to more senators and followed his serious illness and a conspiracy.

questions.stem: In The Roman Revolution (1939), Ronald Syme argued that Augustus:
options: was a faction leader whose rule was a monarchy behind republican forms
sincerely restored the Republic and then retired from political life
was a puppet of Cleopatra, who ruled the empire from Alexandria
inherited a stable Republic that needed no change at all
questions.explanation: Syme saw Augustus as a ruthless party leader who seized power with his faction and disguised a monarchy behind restored republican institutions. Other historians stress the genuine consent and stability Augustus achieved, so the interpretation is debated.
